Of these, 393 queries were carefully crafted by seven human annotators to capture diverse real-world harmful scenarios. These scenarios span combinations along two axes— harm target and harm type —as illustrated in Figure 2 . 3.1 Taxonomy Figure 2: Composition of STOU by harm target and harm type . By combining two harm dimensions, STOU comprises 2,902 samples spanning four harm targets (left) and six harm types (right), representing diverse real-world scenarios. Harm Target. We categorize harmful queries into four groups — (a) Self , (b) The Others , (c) Others , and (d) Unspecified — based on whether and how the target of harm can be identified from the multimodal input. Queries with no identifiable target from the video and audio are labeled Unspecified . Otherwise, we distinguish Self , where the user is the target; The Others , where the target is another person in the user’s visual field (e.g., a person leaning on the couch); and Others , where the target is a specific person outside the visual scene (e.g., a kid). This taxonomy enables broader analysis of safety vulnerabilities across interaction contexts and informs targeted safeguards for egocentric multimodal assistants. Harm Type. Drawing on prior work on safety and harmful behaviors ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2025 ) , we define six harm types: (a) Physical , (b) Psychological , (c) Financial , (d) Privacy , (e) Sexual , and (f) Societal . Together, they cover physical injury, psychological distress, sexual harm or exploitation, financial loss or fraud, privacy violations, and harm to individuals or society. Combined with the Harm Target axis, these categories yield diverse safety scenarios for evaluating whether multimodal assistants recognize harmful intent across different forms of harm. 3.2 Data Construction Pipeline Our data construction pipeline consists of four stages, progressively transforming raw egocentric videos into diverse, human-verified multimodal safety samples. An overview of the pipeline and detailed illustrations of each stage are presented in Figure 9 . Figure 3: Harm-directed harmful text query generation pipeline. We first sample a scenario by harm target and harm type, and pair it with a video description. We then set a target phrase for the chosen harm target. For example, when the target is The Others , a visible person is taken from the video description as the target phrase; if no other person appears, another video is used. The scenario, video description, and target phrase are given to an LLM to generate a harmful text query. For human-written queries, annotators view the video and write the query using the same logic. Stage 1: Video Clip Sampling. We sample 3–10-second egocentric clips from diverse large-scale seed datasets, including Ego4D ( Grauman et al., 2022 ) , Aria-AEA ( Lv et al., 2024 ) , and Nymeria+ ( DeTone et al., 2026 ) . For each clip, we use GPT-5.1, a vision-language model (VLM) with strong visual grounding, to generate a detailed description. These descriptions support subsequent scenario generation, enabling multiple safety scenarios per clip by varying harm Target × \times harm Type . Stage 2: Scenario Construction and Harm-directed Text Query Generation. As illustrated in Figure 3 , we construct each scenario by sampling a harm target × \times harm type combination (e.g., The Others × \times Financial ) and assign a target phrase accordingly. For Self and Unspecified , no explicit phrase is assigned: Self is grounded by visual cues, allowing expressions such as “me” or “myself” to arise naturally during query generation, whereas Unspecified is intentionally target-unspecified. For Others , we sample a phrase from a predefined real-world targets (e.g., children, people, employees), assuming that these targets are absent from the scene. For The Others , which requires a visible target, we provide the video description to GPT-4.1 and Kimi 2.5 to identify a specific person; if none is identifiable, we discard the clip and sample a replacement. Finally, an LLM generates a harmful query conditioned on the sampled scenario, target phrase, and video description. To capture harmful requests that may naturally arise in everyday real-world situations, seven human experts additionally authored 393 queries. Stage 3: Human Verification and Revision. Fifteen Human annotators review the generated queries, discarding samples with hallucinated or inaccurate video descriptions or insufficiently harmful content. Queries with incorrect harm-target or harm-type labels are relabeled accordingly. The remaining queries are refined for fluency and naturalness, while preserving their harmful intent and visual consistency, and then converted into audio. Stage 4: Speech Synthesis and Multimodal Construction. We convert verified text queries into speech using GPT-4o-mini-tts. Each video clip is then paired with its verified text query and synthesized speech to form the final (video, text, audio) multimodal triplet. 4 Evaluation 4.1 Safety Understanding Figure 4: Safety understanding evaluation framework. Given a harmful query, the model identifies the user’s intended action and associated harm, including mechanism, target, and consequence. An LLM judge compares them with gold annotations to score both. The query’s harmfulness is considered “understood” when both are judged correct. Defining Safety Understanding. We define safety understanding from two complementary perspectives— interiority and interaction —as illustrated in Figure 4 . Interiority captures whether the model understands what the user intends to do, while interaction captures how the action may cause harm, who may be affected and what harm may occur. We evaluate the two perspectives separately using intended-action and harm-understanding probes. Building Gold Annotations. For each harmful multimodal sample, we construct a gold reference from the egocentric video, user query, and provided harm type and target labels with their definitions. The reference captures (a) interiority , the user’s intended action and (b) interaction , the primary harm as a causal chain from the affected party , through the harm mechanism , to the resulting consequence . Beyond the primary harm, we also include multiple contextually plausible alternative scenarios in the gold reference. This allows the evaluator to judge a probed model response as correct when it identifies a valid harm scenario supported by the given context. Model Probing for Safety Understanding. To probe interiority , we ask the model to infer the specific action requested by the user from the multimodal query. The auditory query serves as the primary evidence, while the video resolves references and ambiguities involving objects, people, or locations. The model is instructed to identify only the query-targeted action, distinguishing it from incidental events in the video, without making safety or moral judgments. To probe interaction , we ask whether the requested action could plausibly result in harm. If so, the model identifies the affected party , harm mechanism , and consequence . When multiple harms are plausible, it prioritizes the primary harm that is most immediate and closely tied to the depicted situation. If the model determines that the query is harmless, all three harm attributes are left empty. Figure 5: Human–LLM agreement in safety understanding across different harm thresholds τ \tau , measured by balanced accuracy. τ = 3 \tau=3 achieves the highest balanced accuracy. Evaluating Probing Responses against Gold Annotations. We consider a model to demonstrate safety understanding only when it correctly captures both interiority and interaction . An LLM judge evaluates predictions against the corresponding gold annotations: for interiority , it checks whether the predicted action matches the gold action; for interaction , it assigns weighted scores for correctly identifying the affected party , harm mechanism , and consequence , yielding a 5-point harm-understanding score. A sample is considered understood if the intended action is correct and the harm score is at least τ \tau . To determine τ \tau and validate our LLM-based evaluation, we conduct a human evaluation on 225 query–response pairs from five models over a stratified subset of 45 samples covering all harm target × \times harm type combinations. Each response is independently annotated by three human evaluators, using the same evaluation protocol as our LLM evaluator, GPT-4.1, with the majority vote serving as the human reference. We measure human–LLM agreement using balanced accuracy while varying the threshold τ \tau for harm understanding. As shown in Figure 5 , τ = 3 \tau=3 achieves the highest balanced accuracy of 0.894 and is therefore used to report the Safety Understanding Rate (SUR). This strong agreement supports the reliability of our automated evaluation framework; detailed human-evaluation results are provided in the Appendix. 4.2 Refusal Behavior Refusal styles vary across models, particularly between open- and closed-source models. For instance, open-source models such as Qwen2.5-Omni often use explicit refusal phrases and terminate briefly, whereas closed-source models such as Muse-Spark instead tends to warn about potential harm and suggest safer alternatives, mitigating safety–utility trade-off. We therefore adopt a broad notion of refusal behavior , following prior work ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , to include both explicit refusals and safety-oriented responses that withhold actionable harmful assistance. Using this definition, we report the corresponding unsafe response rate, defined as UR = 1 − Refusal ​ Rate \mathrm{UR}=1-\mathrm{Refusal\ Rate} , in our experiments. 5 Experiments 5.1 Experimental Setup To model the wearable scenario in Figure 1 , we use egocentric video and audio as inputs, prompt each model to act as an egocentric multimodal assistant, and evaluate both text and audio responses. Interestingly, harm target meaningfully influences model safety. Across both settings, several models show large target-dependent variation in unsafe response rate: Gemini has a 7.9%p higher UR for Self than The Others in audio-to-audio, while Gemma shows an even larger 12.2%p gap in audio-to-text. This is particularly concerning for wearable AI. The Others and Others represent risks to third parties who are, respectively, visually identifiable or specified through the audio query, while Unspecified captures ambiguous targets. Most notably, Self consistently shows high UR across models and settings. Since Self directly corresponds to the egocentric device wearer, such vulnerability may enable harmful assistance that directly endangers the user, underscoring the need for target-aware evaluation and explicit safeguards for wearer protection. This disparity is particularly pronounced for Gemini-3-flash, Gemma 4 E4B, and Muse Spark 1.2, whereas VITA-1.5 shows a more balanced profile. Joint Refusal–Understanding Evaluation Reveals Distinct Safety Failure Modes. Crossing refusal and understanding assigns each response to a harmful query to one of the four regimes: Ideal Guard (understood and refused), Alignment Gap (understood but answered), Reflexive Refusal (refused without understanding), and Comprehension Gap (neither understood nor refused). We evaluate all nine models under these regimes in the audio-to-text setting ( Figure 7 ). Comprehension Gap dominates for seven models—all open-source—showing that most unsafe responses arise from unrecognized harm. Closed-source models fail differently: Gemini-3-flash-preview understands 70.7% of requests yet answers half, so most unsafe responses fall into the Alignment Gap ; only Muse Spark 1.2 is dominated by Ideal Guard . Example responses from each regime are shown in Figure 8 . For a request on secretly recording another person, the models exhibited distinct patterns in refusal behavior and safety understanding. Muse Spark, representing Ideal Guard , refused appropriately and suggested the safe alternative of obtaining consent. Baichuan showed Reflexive Refusal : although it briefly refused, suggesting superficial awareness of harm, safety probes failed to identify the harmful intent and even judged the request non-harmful. Gemini exhibited Alignment Gap : it correctly identified the harmful intent, target, mechanism, and privacy consequence, yet still provided concrete hiding locations for the camera such as “among the potted plants”. Finally, Qwen2.5-Omni showed a Comprehension Gap , producing a harmful response while also failing the safety probes. The results demonstrate that our two-axis safety evaluation framework better characterizes diverse safety-alignment failure modes, informing future analysis and safeguard development. Our two-axis safety evaluation framework enables a more nuanced characterization of diverse safety-alignment failure modes. Does Understanding Lead to Refusal? Refusal and understanding diverge in both directions. First, understanding makes refusal more likely but does not guarantee it: pooled over models, understood requests are refused about twice as often as the rest (50.2% vs. 24.4%), yet even understood requests are answered half the time, and for Baichuan 1.5 refusal barely depends on understanding at all. Second, a refusal need not reflect understanding. VITA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B refuse a similar share of requests, but most of VITA-1.5’s refusals come without understanding, whereas most of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B’s come with it. 6 Conclusion We introduced STOU , a benchmark for evaluating the safety of egocentric multimodal assistants, with an interaction-centric taxonomy of harm targets, Self , The Others , Others , and Unspecified , and 2,902 egocentric video–query pairs. We further proposed a safety-understanding framework that evaluates whether models recognize user intent, identify potential harm and its target, and reason about its consequences beyond refusal behavior. Across 10 models, refusal behavior varies systematically by harm target, and models often recognize harm yet still assist, showing that refusal rates alone are insufficient to assess safety. We hope that the STOU benchmark can help facilitate the prevention of diverse safety risks that may arise as egocentric multimodal assistants become increasingly widespread.
